text:
Our People
      Meet the Team
      
      
        Click on a team member to learn more about their research and background.
      
    

    
    

    
    

      
      
        ×
        
        Prof. Rendani Mbuvha
        Lab Director & Professor
        
          Bayesian Methods
          Machine Learning
          Climate Risk
          Actuarial Science
        
        
           
  
    in
    id
    web
  
        
        
          Prof. Rendani Mbuvha serves as Lab Director and brings extensive cross-sector experience spanning academia, industry, and international research institutions. He is a qualified actuary, holding fellowships from both the CSIR, Institute and Faculty of Actuaries (UK) and the Actuarial Society of South Africa Actuarial Society of South Africa (FASSA) since 2015, along with the Chartered Enterprise Risk Actuary designation. His academic credentials include a BSc in Actuarial Science and Statistics from the University of Cape Town (2008–2011), an MSc in Machine Learning from KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm (2015–2017), and a PhD in Artificial Intelligence from the University of Johannesburg  (2018–2021), where he was supported by a 2019 Google Africa PhD Fellowship.
          
          He joined WITS as a lecturer in 2017, progressing to Associate Professor by 2022. Simultaneously, he has held positions as Google DeepMind Academic Fellow at Queen Mary University of London (2022–present), Research Fellow in AI and Applied Statistics at the United Nations University Institute for Water, Environment and Health in Canada (2024–present), and since January 2025, Associate Professor in Actuarial Science at the University of Manchester. He is also co-founder of AfriClimate AI, a grassroots community advancing AI applications for climate resilience across Africa.
          His research output is substantial,over 30 peer-reviewed publications spanning seasonal forecasting, Bayesian neural networks, Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods, and actuarial applications of machine learning. He is co-author of the book Hamiltonian Monte Carlo Methods in Machine Learning (Elsevier, 2023) and has received recognition including the Mail & Guardian 200 Young South Africans award and the International Association of Consulting Actuaries Best Paper Award (2020). His work connects methodological innovation in computational statistics with pressing challenges in climate risk, public health, and insurance.
        
      

      
      
        ×
        
        Dr. Raeesa Manjoo-Docrat
        Senior Researcher & Lecturer
        
          Spatial Statistics
          Infectious Disease Modelling
          Epidemiology
          Stochastic Processes
        
        
        
  
    in
    id
  
        
        
          Dr. Raeesa Manjoo-Docrat has been a lecturer at WITS since 2018, following an impressive academic trajectory marked by multiple accolades. She holds a BSc in Mathematics, a Postgraduate Diploma in Actuarial Science and Mathematical Statistics, and dual Honours degrees in Mathematics and Statistics, the latter earning her the Liberty Medal for best honours student. She completed her MSc in Mathematical Statistics with distinction in 2018, focusing on stochastic processes and generating functions in branching processes. Her PhD, completed in 2022, centred on spatio-stochastic modelling of infectious diseases.
          Her research sits at the intersection of infectious disease dynamics and spatial statistics, with particular attention to heterogeneous populations. She has collaborated with researchers at the CSIR, University of Pretoria, and the South African Medical Research Council on COVID-19 modelling using both spatial and national frameworks. Her 2025 open-access publication in CSIR, Heliyon on spatial modelling of the South African pandemic response exemplifies her approach: integrating mathematical rigour with pressing public health questions. She also spent a year as a postdoctoral fellow at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health from 2023 to 2024, expanding her work on applied epidemiological modelling.
          Beyond research, she teaches applied statistics, spatial statistics, and survival analysis at undergraduate and postgraduate levels. She is an active member of R-Ladies, where she has led sessions on RShiny development and SIR model implementation, and serves as a mentor with the  STEM MentHer programme. She has also co-organised and judged DataFest, a national student data challenge. Outside academia, she runs long-distance and bakes,pursuits she describes as the right balance of endurance and creativity.
        
      

      
      
        ×
        
        Dr. Justine Nasejje
        Postdoctoral Researcher
        
          Survival Analysis
          Machine Learning
          Neural Networks
          Biostatistics
        
        
        
  
    in
    id
  
        
        
          Dr. Justine Nasejje serves as Senior Lecturer at WITS, where she specialises in survival analysis and machine learning methods. Her academic journey began in Uganda, where she completed her BSc in Education at Makerere University in 2007, supported by a government bursary. She chose to major in Mathematics rather than the more popular Economics track, a decision that raised eyebrows among her peers. She subsequently received a scholarship to the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences (AIMS) in 2012, followed by an MSc and PhD at the University of KwaZulu-Natal funded by DAAD. Her 2018 doctoral thesis on random survival forests earned the Kambule Doctoral Award, and her work has since appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology and  BMC Public Health.
          Her current research focuses on developing neural network methods for survival analysis, extending her earlier applications of machine learning to under-five mortality studies in Uganda. She has been a member of the International Biometric Society since 2015 and has held research positions at institutions including the Leibniz-Institut für Präventionsforschung und Epidemiologie in Bremen, Germany. Her contributions have been recognised through awards from the London Mathematical Society (2023) and The World Academy of Sciences (2019).
          Alongside her academic work, she co-founded Tendeka, an initiative providing mentorship and financial support to girls from underprivileged backgrounds. Her own experiences navigating STEM as a young woman inform her commitment to addressing the structural barriers that exclude women from the field.

        Dr. Raeesa Ganey
        Lecturer & Researcher
        
          Multivariate Analysis
          Data Visualisation
          Biplots
          Statistical Education
        
        
        
  
    in
    id

          Dr. Raeesa Ganey has been part of the WITS community since 2015, when she joined the School of Statistics and Actuarial Science as a lecturer. Her academic path began at North-West University in Potchefstroom, where she completed her BSc in Actuarial Science back in 2011. She then headed south to the University of Cape Town, spending the next several years immersed in postgraduate studies,wrapping up her Honours in 2012, Master's in 2014, and eventually her PhD in 2019.
          These days she teaches second-year Mathematical Statistics and third-year Multivariate Data Analysis, a course she actually introduced at the honours level after completing her doctorate. Her research sits at the intersection of multivariate analysis and visualisation, she's particularly known for her work on biplots, where she's developed new ways to capture non-linear patterns in complex data. Beyond WITS, she collaborates with Stellenbosch University's visualisation group and stays active in the South African Statistical Association.

  Odey Mofokeng
  Masters Student in Statistics

    Odey Mofokeng is an MSc student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where his dissertation develops a Multidimensional Climate Risk Scorecard using a Bayesian Spatial Copula framework for insurance pricing and sustainability strategy in KwaZulu-Natal. His honours research - Refining Wastewater Surveillance through Regression Kriging: A Geostatistical Approach to Improve Spatial Prediction and Public Health Applications, undertaken in collaboration with the SEPIMOD research group - earned the Peter Fridjhon Gold Medal for Best Honours Research Project, the Liberty Sandton City Voucher for Best Honours Mathematical Statistics Student, First Prize for Best Poster at the 2025 South African Statistical Association Annual Conference, and Third Prize in the SASA Honours Project Competition (2025/26). He also the SAADP Executive Director's Exceptional Diamond Award (2026).
    He holds a BSc in Actuarial Science and a BSc Honours in Mathematical Statistics with distinction, both from the University of the Witwatersrand. His broader interest lies in translating advanced statistical methods into practical tools for climate risk, public health, and insurance.

  Aphiwe Ngcobo
  Honours Student in Mathematical Statistics
  
    Climate Risk
    Health Statistics

    in
  

  
    Aphiwe Ngcobo is an Honours student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where his research focuses on climate exposure and health risk in Gauteng - examining how extreme heat, drought, and heavy rainfall affect vulnerable populations in the region. His project brings together climate data with public health analysis, applying statistical methods to questions of growing urgency as South Africa's climate shifts.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025. Alongside his studies he has been active in the Wits chess, astronomy, investment, and coding societies. He describes himself as a disciplined and dedicated actuary in the making, and his Honours research reflects a commitment to using quantitative methods for real-world social impact.

  Jessie Leukes
  Masters Student in Statistics
  
    Biplots
    Multivariate Analysis
    Statistical Computing
    Goodness-of-Fit
  
  
  
  
    in
  
  
  
    Jessie Leukes is an MSc student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where her research focuses on developing measures of fit for Canonical Variate Analysis biplots based on the Generalised Singular Value Decomposition. Her work sits at the intersection of multivariate statistical theory and practical visualisation tools, aiming to provide more robust diagnostics for assessing how well these biplots represent the underlying data structure.
    She holds a BCom Honours in Statistics from Stellenbosch University, which she completed cum laude in 2022, and a BCom in Investment Management and Statistics, also cum laude, from the same institution. Her academic achievements include the Rector's Award for Excellent Achievement (2022), recognition as the Top Final Year Student in Statistics (2021), Top Second Year Student in Economics (2020), and Top Second Year Student in Financial Accounting (2020).
    Alongside her studies, Jessie works as a Quantitative Analyst at Nedbank in the Advanced Analytics and Innovation division within Group Risk Analytics, a role she has held since October 2024. Before joining the banking sector, she gained early exposure to quantitative finance through an internship at Coronation Fund Managers, where she worked in the Investment Risk and Performance team. Her combination of industry experience and academic rigour brings a practical perspective to her research on statistical methodology.

  Awelani Phaswana
  Masters Student in Statistics
  
    Time Series
    Forecasting
    Energy Markets
    Multivariate Methods
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Awelani Phaswana is an MSc student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where her research focuses on forecasting electricity prices in South Africa using multivariate approaches. Her work brings together time series methodology and the practical realities of the South African energy market, an area of growing importance as the country navigates a rapidly changing power landscape.
    She holds a BBusSci in Statistical Science, Finance and Economics from the University of Cape Town, completed in 2012. She began her career at Eskom as a Graduate in Training in Statistics in 2013, and over the following decade has built substantial experience across forecasting, business intelligence, and management consulting. She held roles as Management Consultant and Senior Consultant within Eskom's Top Consulting Group before serving as Acting Programme Manager and then Chief Advisor in Business Intelligence.
    In September 2022 she was appointed Forecasting Manager within the Energy Trading division, and in December 2025 she took up the role of Demand and Price Forecasting Executive, where she leads forecasting functions at a national level. Her return to formal postgraduate study reflects a commitment to grounding her industry expertise in rigorous statistical methodology, and her research is directly informed by the operational demands of forecasting in one of South Africa's most critical sectors.

    Lazola Ntanjana is an MSc student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where his research focuses on a Generalised Singular Value Decomposition (GSVD) approach to MANOVA for high-dimensional data.
    He holds a BSc Honours in Statistics (2024) and a BSc in Actuarial Science and Mathematical Statistics (2020–2023), both from the University of the Witwatersrand. His academic background combines the rigour of actuarial training with a strong foundation in statistical theory and computation.
    Alongside his studies, Lazola works as a Quantitative Analyst at FNB South Africa, where he is part of the Broader Africa / FNB International Credit Retail Impairment team. He joined the bank through the FNB Graduate Programme in January 2025 and transitioned into a permanent quantitative analyst role in January 2026. His day-to-day work in credit impairment modelling complements his research interests in multivariate methods, and his industry experience brings a practical dimension to his work.

    Nontsikelelo Wittes is an Honours student in Data Science at WITS, where her research investigates the effect of risk set sampling on Random Forest Survival models in the presence of censoring.
    She holds a BSc in Computational and Applied Mathematics from the University of the Witwatersrand. Her training in computational methods and applied mathematics underpins her interest in machine learning methodology. Beyond her academic work, Nontsikelelo serves as a Director at the Heart Of Hope Foundation, a South African organisation supporting children and community welfare.

    Steven Mphaya is a PhD candidate in Statistical Data Science, where his research focuses on deep learning for modelling ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) scores and risk measures. He holds an MSc in Mathematics and Statistics from the University of Cape Coast in Ghana (2021–2022) and a Bachelor's degree in Mathematical Sciences from the University of Malawi (2015–2020). He is currently completing a PhD at the Università degli Studi di Salerno in Italy (2023–2026), complementing his research at WITS.
    
    Alongside his doctoral work, Steven is a Staff Associate and researcher with experience in credit risk and cloud data analytics. He has completed further professional training including a Postgraduate Course in Econometrics from the Italian Econometric Association (2024), a Certificate in Urban Economics from the Bureau for Research and Economic Analysis of Development and the International Growth Centre (2024).

    Daniel Morris is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research asks a question with real consequences for market participants: Should I trust my sell-side analyst? Working alongside Jonathan Stagman, his project examines the reliability of analyst forecasts and recommendations.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand with distinction in 2025. Alongside his studies, Daniel has built practical experience in quantitative finance — at Eau Rouge Investment Managers he designed a quantitative screening and ranking system covering all JSE-listed companies, and he has also worked as a valuation consultant developing full business valuations.

Their project brings quantitative methods to bear on the reliability of analyst forecasts and recommendations.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand with distinction in 2025. He is now completing his Honours degree, with his research applying statistical rigour to questions at the intersection of actuarial science and financial markets.

    Gianluca Caldeira is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Rhys Meyer - examines the natural disaster impacts on residential property prices in South Africa. Focusing on the 2017 Knysna fires and the KwaZulu-Natal floods, their project quantifies how extreme events feed through into housing valuations, a question of growing importance as climate risk reshapes property markets across the country.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025 and is now completing his Honours degree. He is also co-founder and director of The Prego Boyz, a food trailer business he ran from 2019 to 2025 that served over 6 500 prego rolls at markets and private events - an enterprise that speaks to his appetite for building things from the ground up.

    Dinal Bhoola is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Wade Reddy - develops a multi-hazard climate risk assessment and examines parametric insurance design for South Africa. His project brings together the actuarial and statistical tools needed to model overlapping climate hazards and to evaluate how index-based insurance structures can transfer risk more efficiently than traditional indemnity products. He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025,  and is now pursuing his Honours degree.

  Wade Reddy
  Honours Student in Actuarial Science
  
    Parametric Insurance
    Copula Methods
    Climate Risk
    Python & Geospatial
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Wade Reddy is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Dinal Bhoola - develops a multi-hazard parametric insurance framework for South Africa. His project is unusually hands-on for an Honours dissertation: using Python (CLIMADA and GeoPandas), he has built an end-to-end risk-transfer architecture, fitted Gamma and GEV marginal distributions with a bivariate Gumbel copula to capture coupled wind-rainfall extremes, and generated a 10 000-event synthetic library with K-means clustering and constrained optimisation to calibrate index triggers, payout factors, and portfolio liability caps.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025. His research reflects a first-principles approach to risk and a commitment to making complex quantitative work actionable for the people who need to act on it.

  Keletso Mabelane

    Keletso Mabelane is an MSc student in Statistics at WITS, where her research focuses on pricing European commodity options using normalising flows. Her work brings modern generative modelling techniques to bear on a classical problem in quantitative finance - moving beyond the restrictive distributional assumptions of Black-Scholes-type models to capture the complex, non-Gaussian behaviour of commodity price dynamics.
    She holds a BSc in Actuarial Science from the University of the Witwatersrand (2019–2021) and a BSc Honours in Mathematical Statistics (2022). In 2022 she co-authored An Analysis of Local Government Financial Statement Audit Outcomes in a Developing Economy Using Machine Learning in Sustainability with Wilson Tsakane Mongwe, Rendani Mbuvha, and Tshilidzi Marwala - an early demonstration of her interest in applying machine learning to public-sector and financial data. Alongside her studies, she works as an Actuarial Analyst at Deloitte, where she has progressed from Junior Actuarial Analyst (2023) to her current role (2024–present).

  Zahir Nikraftar
  PhD Candidate in Computer Science
  
    Deep Learning
    Seasonal Forecasting
    Geospatial AI
    Climate Extremes
  

  
  
    in
    id
  

  
    Zahir Nikraftar is a PhD candidate in Computer Science at Queen Mary University of London, funded by a Google DeepMind studentship. His research develops advanced deep learning architectures - Transformers, diffusion models, and large-scale CNNs - for high-dimensional geoscientific and climate data, trained at scale on multi-GPU HPC clusters. Within the lab, he is the lead author on Season-Net, a deep learning framework for bias correction of seasonal forecasting models, developed with Prof. Rendani Mbuvha and collaborators at the South African Weather Service and University of Cape Town.
    
    His publication record spans 19 works in hydrology, remote sensing, and climate science, including articles in Journal of Hydrology, Earth's Future, Remote Sensing, and Environmental Data Science. Two threads run through this body of work: an early focus on water systems and drought - Urmia Lake restoration, groundwater sustainability using GRACE/GRACE-FO data, multi-type global drought assessment - and a more recent turn towards machine learning for climate prediction, including impact-based skill evaluation of seasonal precipitation forecasts and interpretable ML frameworks for soil moisture dynamics, both co-authored with Mbuvha.
    
    Alongside his PhD, Zahir is a Senior Machine Learning Scientist at Outbreak Labs in London, and previously led AI development at Permia Sensing, building deep learning pipelines for satellite and UAV imagery analysis. He also worked as a Machine Learning Researcher with AfriClimate AI, and has production experience architecting LLM and RAG systems for enterprise applications. His combination of climate science, deep learning methodology, and applied engineering makes him a natural bridge between the lab's research agenda and real-world deployment.

  Annine Duclaire Kenne
  PhD Candidate in Statistics
  
    Seasonal Forecasting

    Annine Duclaire Kenne is a PhD candidate in Statistics working within the lab, where her research focuses on advancing seasonal weather risk assessment using machine learning. Her work applies deep learning and time series methods to the problem of improving the reliability of seasonal forecasts - a question with direct consequences for agriculture, water management, and disaster preparedness across Africa.
    Her academic path has moved from physics into machine learning. She holds a Bachelor's and Master's degree in Physics (Fundamental Mechanics and Complex Systems) from the University of Yaoundé I, before completing a Master's in Mathematical Sciences with a Big-Data specialisation at the African Institute for Mathematical Sciences (AIMS), where her thesis focused on predicting drought over Cameroon using machine learning. She has since held a research position as an ML Researcher at Johannes Kepler Universität Linz in Austria (2023–2025) and is completing the African Masters of Machine Intelligence programme. Her research interests span climate change, time series, computer vision, and optimisation.
    Alongside her research, Annine is committed to making quantitative science accessible. She has served as a Data Science Mentor at the Webber Institute of Technology, has taught physics and chemistry at the secondary level, and has volunteered through AIMS outreach programmes raising awareness of STEM among high school students in Cameroon. Her combination of physics training, machine learning expertise, and a genuine investment in teaching gives her research a grounded, collaborative character.

  Abdoulaye Diop
  PhD Candidate in Statistics
  
    Climate Health
    Early Warning Systems
    Multi-Hazard Risk
    Climate Data Science
  

  
  
    in
    rg
  

  
    Abdoulaye Diop is a PhD candidate in Statistics at The University of Manchester, where his research sits at the intersection of climate-related health and sustainable development. He joined the university in April 2026, building on a master's thesis that assessed multi-hazard risks to maize, millet, and cowpea yields in the Sahel - work completed through the WASCAL Graduate Studies Programme at the École Doctorale Informatique et Changement Climatique, Université Joseph KI-ZERBO in Burkina Faso.
    
    He has built a short-range precipitation forecasting pipeline for Senegal using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model, and completed NASA ARSET training on extreme weather statistics using downscaled CMIP6 projections. Earlier roles include Climate Change Analyst at Université Joseph KI-ZERBO and an internship with WASCAL, the West African Science Service Centre on Climate Change and Adapted Land Use. His research is motivated by a clear practical goal: high-resolution forecasting and hazard assessment that can support agriculture, disaster risk reduction, and early warning systems across Africa.

  Kopano Motebu
  Honours Student in Mathematical Statistics
  
    Forecast Skill
    AI Weather Models

    Climate Science
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Kopano Motebu is an Honours student in Mathematical Statistics at WITS, where his research focuses on the statistical characterisation of forecast skill decay in AI-based medium-range weather models. His project examines how the predictive accuracy of machine learning weather models degrades with forecast horizon - a question of increasing importance as AI systems begin to challenge traditional numerical weather prediction in operational settings. He holds a BSc in Actuarial Science from the University of the Witwatersrand, completed in 2025. He is now pursuing his Honours degree in Mathematical Statistics.
  




  ×
  
  Luke Cable
  Honours Student in Actuarial Science
  
    Heat Stress
    Labour Productivity
    Crop Yields
    Climate Risk
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Luke Cable is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Luthando Zondi - examines the impacts of heat stress on labour productivity and crop yields in South Africa. Their project quantifies how rising temperatures feed through into two critical dimensions of economic and social vulnerability: the capacity of workers to perform physical labour under heat, and the viability of agricultural output in a warming climate.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand with distinction in 2025. Outside academia, he is a keen runner, mountain biker, hiker, and saxophonist, and has volunteered with parkrun since 2019.
  





  ×
  
  Luthando Zondi
  Honours Student in Actuarial Science
  
    Climate Risk
    CLIMADA
    Crop Yields
    Labour Productivity
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Luthando Zondi is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Luke Cable - examines the heat stress impact on crop yields and labour productivity in South Africa using the CLIMADA framework. Their work applies a probabilistic catastrophe modelling platform to quantify how extreme heat feeds through into agricultural output and workforce capacity, a question with direct relevance for insurers, agribusinesses, and policymakers preparing for a warming climate.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025. Alongside his studies he has gained practical exposure through an AIG actuarial analyst job simulation (marine liability pricing) and a vacation programme with True South Actuaries. Outside academia, he is co-founder of Tsebo Academic Excellence, where he tutors grade 10 and 11 learners and helps recruit teachers, and he plays football for the Wits Football Club.
  




  ×
  
  Rohan Bodalina
  Honours Student in Actuarial Science
  
    Mortality Forecasting
    Recurrent Neural Networks
    Deep Learning
    Actuarial Science
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Rohan Bodalina is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Jolan Govender - develops mortality forecasting models using recurrent neural networks. Their project applies deep learning to one of the oldest problems in actuarial science: projecting future mortality rates with sufficient accuracy to inform life insurance pricing, reserving, and longevity risk management. RNNs offer a natural fit for the sequential structure of mortality time series, and their work explores how these architectures compare with established stochastic mortality models.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025 and is now pursuing his Honours degree. Outside his studies he plays violin and golf - pursuits he describes as keeping a good balance between focus and creativity. His approach to actuarial work emphasises problem-solving through real-world challenges, and his research reflects that same orientation towards practical applications of modern methods.
  





  ×
  
  Jolan Govender
  Honours Student in Actuarial Science
  
    Mortality Forecasting
    LSTM & GRU Networks
    Lee-Carter Model
    Pensions
  

  
  
    in
  

  
    Jolan Govender is an Honours student in Actuarial Science at WITS, where his research - undertaken with Rohan Bodalina - benchmarks recurrent neural network architectures against the Lee-Carter model for long-horizon mortality forecasting, with implications for defined benefit pension scheme valuations. He constructed and evaluated LSTM and GRU networks on a 10-year out-of-sample test set. The findings were instructive rather than confirmatory: Lee-Carter outperformed both RNN architectures overall, with the networks producing notably flat long-horizon trajectories that failed to capture sustained mortality improvement trends. A notable exception emerged in Japanese female mortality data, where the LSTM outperformed Lee-Carter - a population-specific dynamic worth exploring further.
    He completed his BSc in Actuarial Science at the University of the Witwatersrand in 2025, with his sights set on the FASSA qualification. His interests lie in the life, health, and pensions space, where rigorous modelling has the most direct bearing on people's long-term financial security. Beyond his research, he placed third on the Risk Cost Leaderboard in the 2026 MiWay Actuarial Hackathon, building an end-to-end predictive model for short-term insurance pricing using GLMs and LightGBMs. Outside of work he plays golf and padel.

      About Us
      Who We Are
      
      
        The WITS Old Mutual Insure Risk Lab is a pioneering research laboratory
        established through a partnership between the University of the
        Witwatersrand's School of Statistics and Actuarial Science and Old Mutual
        Insure.
      
    

    
      
        
         🎯
          
            Our Mission
            
              To solve complex risk problems facing African communities and industries through rigorous quantitative research. We develop methods that work in practice, not just in theory, and ensure our findings reach those who can use them.

About Us
      Who We Are
      
      
        The WITS Old Mutual Insure Risk Lab is a pioneering research laboratory
        established through a partnership between the University of the
        Witwatersrand's School of Statistics and Actuarial Science and Old Mutual
        Insure. We are dedicated to producing impactful research tackling climate risk, infectious disease modelling, and sustainable insurance through advanced statistical and machine learning methods.
      
    

    
      
      
        
          🎯
          
            Our Mission
            
              To solve complex risk problems facing African communities and industries 
          through rigorous quantitative research. We develop methods that work in 
          practice, not just in theory, and ensure our findings reach those who can 
          use them.
            
          
        

        
          🌍

title: Research
text:
Research Focus
      Our Research Areas
      
      
        Our research spans a broad spectrum of statistical and actuarial
        disciplines, united by the goal of advancing quantitative risk
        assessment methodologies.
      
    

    
  
  
    
      🌡️
      Climate Risk Modelling
      
        Developing spatial and temporal models for extreme weather events,
        seasonal forecasting, and climate-resilient insurance pricing across
        African regions. This includes heatwaves, drought, and flood risk assessment.
      
    
  

  
  
    
     🧠
      Machine Learning & AI
      
        Applying deep learning, neural networks, and ensemble methods to
        insurance and health datasets for improved prediction and risk classification.
        We explore supervised and unsupervised learning for actuarial applications.
      
    
  

  
  
    
      🏥
      Health & Survival Analysis
      
        Studying mortality trends, infectious disease dynamics, and longevity risk
        using survival analysis and machine learning methods. This includes
        under-five mortality, maternal health, and Bayesian mortality projections.
      
    
  

  
  
    
      🗺️
      Spatial Statistics
      
        Using geostatistical methods, kriging, and spatial copula frameworks for
        environmental monitoring, regional risk mapping, and wastewater surveillance.
        This includes Bayesian spatial modelling for public health and insurance.
      
    
  

  
  
    
      📊
      Data Visualisation
      
        Developing multivariate visualisation techniques including biplots,
principal surfaces, and goodness-of-fit diagnostics. This includes
interactive dashboards using RShiny for exploring high-dimensional data.
      
    
  

  
  
    
    🛡️
      Risk & Insurance Analytics
      
        Developing pricing, reserving, and capital assessment models for
        general and life insurance. This includes catastrophe modelling,
        dependence structures, and stochastic simulations for portfolio risk.
      
    
  
  
    
  
    
      📐
      Multivariate Methods
      
        Extending classical multivariate techniques to high-dimensional settings,
        including Generalised Singular Value Decomposition (GSVD) approaches to
        MANOVA and Canonical Variate Analysis, with applications to complex
        actuarial and financial data.
      
    
  
  
    
  
    
      ⚡
      Energy & Financial Forecasting
      
        Developing multivariate time series methods for forecasting electricity
        prices, demand, and financial market variables in South African and
        African markets. This includes regime-switching models and dependence
        structures in energy portfolios.
      
    
    
  
       
       
       



  
    
      Current Work
      Projects in Progress
      
      
        The lab is establishing its research programme. Current student
        projects are underway, with outputs expected in the coming years.
      
    

    
      
        

          
            
              Climate Risk and Insurance Pricing
            
            
              Odey Mofokeng (MSc Statistics) is developing Bayesian spatial
              copula frameworks for insurance pricing in KwaZulu-Natal,
              examining flood and drought risk through geostatistical methods. Expected completion: December 2026
            
          

          
            
              Climate Exposure and Health Risk
            
            
              Aphiwe Ngcobo (Honours Statistics) is examining how extreme heat,
              drought, and heavy rainfall affect vulnerable populations in
              Gauteng, combining climate data with public health analysis. Expected completion: December 2026
            
          
          
                    
            
              Multivariate Methods for High-Dimensional Data
            
            
              Lazola Ntanjana (MSc Statistics) is developing a Generalised
              Singular Value Decomposition (GSVD) approach to MANOVA for
              high-dimensional data. Expected completion: February 2027.
            
          

          
            
              Forecasting South African Electricity Prices
            
            
              Awelani Phaswana (MSc Statistics) is developing multivariate
              approaches for forecasting electricity prices in South Africa,
              combining time series methodology with the realities
              of the energy market. Expected completion: December 2027.
            
          

          
            
              Goodness-of-Fit for Canonical Variate Analysis Biplots
            
            
              Jessie Leukes (MSc Statistics) is developing measures of fit for
              Canonical Variate Analysis biplots based on the Generalised
              Singular Value Decomposition, providing robust diagnostics for
              assessing how well these biplots represent the underlying data
              structure. Expected completion: December 2027.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Risk Set Sampling in Random Survival Forests
            
            
              Nontsikelelo Wittes (Honours Data Science) is investigating the
              effect of risk set sampling on Random Forest Survival models in
              the presence of censoring, examining how sampling choices at each
              event time influence model performance and stability.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Deep Learning for ESG Scores and Risk Measures
            
            
              Steven Mphaya (PhD Statistical Data Science) is developing deep
              learning methods for modelling ESG scores and risk measures,
              exploring how neural network architectures can capture the complex,
              multidimensional relationships underlying sustainability ratings
              and their implications for financial risk.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Should I Trust My Sell-Side Analyst?
            
            
              Daniel Morris and Jonathan Stagman (Honours Actuarial Science) are
              investigating the reliability of sell-side analyst forecasts and
              recommendations.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Natural Disaster Impacts on Residential Property Prices
            
            
              Gianluca Caldeira and Rhys Meyer (Honours Actuarial Science) are
              investigating how natural disasters affect residential property
              prices in South Africa, using the 2017 Knysna fires and the
              KwaZulu-Natal floods as case studies.
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Multi-Hazard Climate Risk and Parametric Insurance
            
            
              Dinal Bhoola and Wade Reddy (Honours Actuarial Science) are
              developing a multi-hazard climate risk assessment for South
              Africa and evaluating parametric insurance structures as a
              mechanism for transferring climate risk.
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Pricing European Commodity Options Using Normalising Flows
            
            
              Keletso Mabelane (MSc Statistics) is developing normalising flow
              methods for pricing European commodity options, moving beyond
              restrictive distributional assumptions to capture the complex
              behaviour of commodity price dynamics.
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Towards More Reliable Seasonal Climate Forecasts
            
            
              Zahir Nikraftar (PhD Computer Science, Queen Mary University of
              London) is developing deep learning methods for bias correction
              of seasonal forecasting models, with the aim of improving the
              reliability of climate forecasts used in risk assessment across
              Africa. His related work with Prof. Rendani Mbuvha on impact-based
              skill evaluation of seasonal precipitation forecasts appeared in
              Earth's Future (2024).
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Advancing Seasonal Weather Risk Assessment Using Machine Learning
            
            
              Annine Duclaire Kenne (PhD Statistics) is developing machine
              learning methods to improve seasonal weather risk assessment,
              building on her earlier work on drought prediction over Cameroon
              and her research on deep learning for climate applications.
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Climate Health Nexus
            
            
              Abdoulaye Diop (PhD Statistics, University of Manchester) is
              researching the intersection of climate-related health and
              sustainable development, building on his WASCAL-funded work on
              multi-hazard risks to staple crop yields in the Sahel and his
              development of high-resolution precipitation forecasting
              pipelines for West Africa.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Forecast Skill Decay in AI-Based Weather Models
            
            
              Kopano Motebu (Honours Mathematical Statistics) is statistically
              characterising how forecast skill decays with lead time in
              AI-based medium-range weather models, examining the practical
              limits of machine learning weather prediction.
            
          
          
          
                    
            
              Heat Stress Impacts on Labour Productivity and Crop Yields
            
            
              Luke Cable and Luthando Zondi (Honours Actuarial Science) are
              examining how heat stress affects labour productivity and crop
              yields in South Africa, quantifying the economic and social
              consequences of rising temperatures.
            
          
          
                    
            
              Mortality Forecasting Using Recurrent Neural Networks
            
            
              Rohan Bodalina and Jolan Govender (Honours Actuarial Science) are
              developing recurrent neural network models for mortality
              forecasting, exploring how deep learning architectures compare
              with established stochastic mortality models for applications in
              life insurance and longevity risk.
            
          
          
          
          
            
              Developing Collaborations
            
            
              We are building partnerships with industry and academic
              institutions to expand our research capacity and create
              opportunities for future publications and conference presentations.
